content: Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological condition, and approximately 30% of individuals with epilepsy are classified as drug-resistant, necessitating treatment with multiple antiepileptic drugs. Perampanel is a newer antiepileptic medication that has been studied as an adjunctive therapy for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The objective of this research was to assess the efficacy and safety of perampanel as an add-on treatment for individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The study utilized rigorous Cochrane search methods, with the most recent search conducted on October 20, 2022. Randomized controlled trials comparing perampanel as an add-on therapy to placebo were included in the analysis. The primary outcome of interest was achieving a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency. Secondary outcomes included seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal for any reason, treatment withdrawal due to adverse effects, and the occurrence of adverse effects. The analysis was conducted using an intention-to-treat approach, and results were presented as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For individual adverse effects, 99% CIs were used to account for multiple testing. The GRADE system was employed to evaluate the certainty of evidence for each outcome. Seven trials involving 2,524 participants aged 12 years and older were included. These trials were double-blind, randomized, and placebo-controlled, with treatment durations ranging from 12 to 19 weeks. Four trials were assessed as having a low risk of bias, while three had an unclear risk of bias due to concerns related to detection, reporting, and other biases. Participants receiving perampanel were significantly more likely to achieve a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to those receiving placebo (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.43 to 1.95; high-certainty evidence). Perampanel also increased the likelihood of seizure freedom compared to placebo (RR 2.50, 95% CI 1.38 to 4.54; low-certainty evidence). However, treatment withdrawal was more common among participants treated with perampanel compared to placebo (RR 1.30, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.63; low-certainty evidence). Specifically, withdrawal due to adverse effects was significantly higher in the perampanel group (RR 2.36, 95% CI 1.59 to 3.51; low-certainty evidence). A greater proportion of participants receiving perampanel reported experiencing one or more adverse effects compared to those on placebo (RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.24; high-certainty evidence). Specific adverse effects associated with perampanel included ataxia (RR 14.32, 99% CI 1.09 to 188.31; low-certainty evidence), dizziness (RR 2.87, 99% CI 1.45 to 5.70; low-certainty evidence), and somnolence (RR 1.76, 99% CI 1.02 to 3.04). Subgroup analysis revealed that perampanel doses of 4 mg/day (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.83), 8 mg/day (RR 1.83, 95% CI 1.51 to 2.22), and 12 mg/day (RR 2.38, 95% CI 1.86 to 3.04) were associated with a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency compared to placebo. However, the 12 mg/day dose was also linked to an increased likelihood of treatment withdrawal (RR 1.77, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.40). In conclusion, perampanel as an add-on therapy is effective in reducing seizure frequency and may help achieve seizure freedom in individuals with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. While generally well-tolerated, perampanel was associated with a higher rate of treatment withdrawals compared to placebo. The 8 mg/day and 12 mg/day doses appear to be the most effective, though the 12 mg/day dose may lead to more treatment discontinuations. Future research should focus on evaluating the long-term efficacy and tolerability of perampanel and determining the optimal dosing strategy.
